title: Cost Tracker
headings: Start with your role# Project owner or manager# Portfolio manager# Finance or analyst# Jira administrator# How the pieces fit# Where to open it#
text: Most cost-tracking apps ask people to log time a second time, inside them. Cost Tracker reads Jira's own worklogs directly. It adds the money layer Jira does not have: what each person costs per hour, what a project has spent and earned, and whether it is on budget. Quick start → How cost is calculated Troubleshooting Start with your role # Project owner or manager # You set up a project and watch it against budget. Quick start Cost projects and scope Rates, roles and the team Expenses , budget , revenue Portfolio manager # You look across several projects. Portfolios Reports Sharing and ownership Finance or analyst # You need to trust the numbers. How cost is calculated Limits and behaviour Glossary Jira administrator # You install the app and manage site-wide setup. Permissions and access Cost accounts Privacy and security How the pieces fit # A cost project is the app's own entity. It is not a copy of a Jira project: it is defined by a scope (one or more Jira spaces, or any JQL filter), and everything else hangs off it. One cost project can span several Jira projects, and one Jira project can be covered by several cost projects. Scope decides which issues, and therefore which worklogs, count. Rates turn each worklog's hours into money. A rate can belong to a person, a role, a cost account or the project, and it can change from a given date. Expenses add costs that worklogs do not capture, such as licences and contractor invoices. Revenue (optional) adds what the project earns, so profit and margin appear next to cost. Budget and milestones (optional) give the cost something to be compared with. Portfolios and reports combine several projects, or slice one by period, person or account. Where to open it # Open Cost Tracker from the Apps menu in the Jira sidebar. The app has one global page with three areas: Workspace (Projects, Portfolios, Reports) and Setup (Accounts, Attributes, Roles). It does not add anything to individual Jira projects.

title: Quick start
headings: The example project# Create the project# Set rates# Check the result# What to add next#
text: The example project # These docs use one small project so the numbers can be followed from page to page. You do not need the same data; any Jira space with a few worklogs will do. Example: Website redesign A monetary project in USD that reads the Jira space WEB . Three people logged time in July 2026: Person Set up as Hours logged Anna Own rate 50/h 10 h Ben Role "Developer" at 40/h 5 h on a CAPEX issue, 5 h on other issues Carol No rate of her own, no role 4 h The project default rate is 30/h, and a cost account "Capitalised work" (JQL labels = capex ) has a rate of 60/h. Create the project # Open Cost Tracker from the Jira Apps menu and choose Create project . Give it a name and a scope : pick the Jira space WEB , or write a JQL filter. The scope is checked against your site before it is saved. Choose the project type . Monetary-based computes cost and budget in a currency from hourly rates. Time-based uses hours only and no rates. You can change this later, but nothing is converted (see changing the type or currency ). Set the currency (USD) and, under Settings → Rates and revenue , a Default hourly rate of 30. Do not skip the default rate. A new monetary project starts with a default rate of 0, so time is counted but priced at 0 until some rate applies. The app shows an "Hourly rates are not set" banner on Overview, Team and Revenue while this is the case. Set rates # Open the Team tab. Everyone who logged time in the scope is already listed. In the Roles card, add the role Developer with a cost rate of 40, then give Ben that role in the table. For Anna, open the ··· menu on her row, choose Edit cost rate and history and enter 50. Leave Effective from empty for now. Create the cost account (a Jira administrator does this under Accounts ): name "Capitalised work", JQL labels = capex , cost rate 60. Check the result # Each worklog takes the first rate that applies, in this order: the person's own rate, the cost account's, the role's, then the project default. For the example: Worklog Rate used Why Cost Anna, 10 h 50 Her own rate wins over everything 500 Ben, 5 h on a CAPEX issue 60 He has no own rate, and the account's rate beats his role 300 Ben, 5 h on other issues 40 No own or account rate, so his role applies 200 Carol, 4 h 30 Nothing else matches, so the project default applies 120 Labor cost 1,120 Open Overview and Team to see the same figures. If cost shows 0, see Troubleshooting . What to add next # Expenses for licences and other costs that are not logged time. A budget to compare cost against. Revenue to see profit and margin. A dated rate when someone's rate changes, so earlier months keep their old price.

title: How cost is calculated
headings: The short version# Pricing one worklog# Project types# What the totals include# Freshness and caching#
text: The short version # The app reads the issues that match the project's scope and the worklogs on them. Each worklog is priced by the rate in force on the day it was logged. The sum of these is the labor cost . Expenses are added. Labor plus expenses is the actual cost . If revenue is tracked, profit is revenue minus actual cost, and margin is profit as a share of revenue. Jira is only read, never changed. Nobody has to log anything in Cost Tracker. Pricing one worklog # Every worklog is priced on its own, not as total hours times one rate. This matters because the same person can be priced differently on different issues (a cost account's rate depends on the issue) and on different dates (a rate can change over time). For each worklog the app takes the first rate it finds, in this order: the person's own rate, the rate of the cost account the issue belongs to, the rate of the person's role, the project's default hourly rate. The date used is the day the worklog was logged for, as Jira stores it. Cost rates and billing rates are resolved separately with the same order. Rates, roles and the team has the full detail and an example. Project types # Type Cost and budget are in Rates Revenue Monetary-based The project's currency Yes Optional Time-based Hours No (the Team tab says so) No, there is no currency to bill in What the totals include # Overview and Team show everything logged on issues in scope. A report lets you pick a timeframe, a breakdown and a filter. Currency is a property of the project. Amounts are never converted between currencies. Issues beyond the limit. A project reads up to 500 issues. If the scope is bigger, the page says "first 500 of about N issues", and the totals are incomplete. See Limits and behaviour . Freshness and caching # Scanning Jira is the slow part, so computed figures are kept for about 15 minutes and recomputed automatically after that. A change that affects the numbers (a rate, a role, a setting, the scope) makes the project recompute straight away. Lists such as the Projects table fill in row by row, so one slow project never blocks the page. If a number looks stale right after you changed something in Jira (for example a worklog you just logged), give it up to 15 minutes. Changes made inside Cost Tracker show immediately.

title: Rates, roles and the team
headings: Who appears on the Team tab# How a rate is chosen# Example# Cost rate and billing rate# Empty is not zero# Roles# Rates that change over time# How to change a rate from a date# Reading the Team tab#
text: This page applies to monetary projects. A time-based project has no rates: the Team tab shows hours only. Roles still work there and feed the "Top roles" breakdown. Who appears on the Team tab # Everyone who logged time in the project's scope appears automatically, plus anyone you add explicitly. A role or a personal rate is optional and never a condition for being counted. You can add people who have not logged anything yet by searching Jira users. Only existing users of your Jira site can be found. The app cannot invite people or send email, so invite a new colleague to the Jira site first. App accounts are not offered. How a rate is chosen # Every worklog is priced individually. For each one the app takes the first rate it finds in this order, and stops: Priority Source Where you set it 1 (highest) The person's own rate Team tab, row menu ··· 2 The rate of the cost account the issue belongs to Accounts (site administrators) 3 The rate of the person's role Team tab, Roles card 4 (fallback) The project's default hourly rate Settings → Rates and revenue A cost account's rate depends on the issue , not the person, so one person can be priced differently on different issues in the same period. The Team table labels each rate by where it came from: their own rate, account , role , default rate , or mixed when an account's rate covered only some of their worklogs. For a person with more than one rate the table shows the average, which is cost divided by hours. Example # Using the example project : Anna's own rate is 50, Ben has no own rate and the role Developer (40), Carol has nothing, the account "Capitalised work" is 60 and the project default is 30. Worklog Rate used Why Cost Anna, 10 h, any issue 50 Her own rate beats the account's 60 and everything else 500 Ben, 5 h, issue in the account 60 No own rate, so the account's rate wins over his role 300 Ben, 5 h, ordinary issue 40 No own or account rate, so his role applies 200 Carol, 4 h 30 Nothing else matches, so the project default applies 120 Cost rate and billing rate # Each person, role and account can carry two rates: a cost rate (what the person costs the business) and a billing rate (what the client is charged). They are resolved independently with the same order, so they can come from different tiers. Billing rates matter only when hourly revenue is on; with a fixed-price project they are hidden. Empty is not zero # Leaving a rate field empty means "not set here, use the next one". Entering 0 means "this work is free" (unpaid or internal work) and is respected as a real rate. Clearing a rate you entered earlier removes it completely and returns the person to the next level; it does not leave a hidden zero. Roles # A role is a named group with a shared cost and billing rate, for example Developer or Designer. Roles belong to one cost project and are not shared between projects. A site administrator can keep a library of common roles (Setup → Roles) that you can quick-pick when adding a role to a project. Deleting a role does not remove its people. They are unassigned and fall to the next level. A role name can be up to 60 characters and must be unique within the project, ignoring case. Picking a role for someone also makes them an explicit team member, because that is where the role is stored. Rates that change over time # Every rate can have a start date: a person's own rate, a role's, a cost account's and the project default. Each worklog is priced by the rate in force on the day it was logged, at every level of the order above. So raising a rate from 1 August leaves July's cost alone. How to change a rate from a date # A person's rate: Team tab, the row's ··· menu, Edit cost rate and history (or billing rate). A role's rate: click the rate on the role's row in the Roles card. The project default: Settings → Rates and revenue → Edit rates and history . A cost account's rate: the account's edit form, Edit rates and history (site administrators). All four open the same window: enter the new rate and, optionally, Effective from . With a date , hours logged on or after that day use the new rate and earlier hours keep their old one. Work logged before a person's first dated rate falls through to the next level. Without a date , the rate applies to all hours, past and future, and replaces the history. An empty rate with a date starts a period with no own rate, so from that day the next level applies. Each period records who set it and when, and the same window lists every period. Saving a form without changing a rate never adds a period or erases the history. Renaming a role is safe. Example: raising the Developer rate Ben's role Developer is 40. On 1 August the rate becomes 45, so you set 45 with Effective from = 1 Aug 2026. His 5 hours on an ordinary issue in July stay at 40 (200); the same hours in August cost 225. Without the date, July would be repriced to 225 as well. Reading the Team tab # You see It means 55 · 2 periods The rate in force today is 55, and this rate has two periods (open the editor to see them). 40 (role) The person has no own rate; their role's 40 applies. default Nothing of their own, no role rate; the project default applies. If hours are counted at 0 only because no rate applies yet, a banner says how many hours. See cost shows 0 .

title: Cost projects and scope
headings: Scope: spaces or JQL# The Projects table# Project tabs# Status, tags and timeframe# Changing the type or currency# Project attributes# Deleting a project#
text: Scope: spaces or JQL # A cost project's scope is set when you create it, from one of two modes, and can be changed later in Settings: Mode What it matches Jira Spaces One or more Jira projects, joined with OR. You pick them from a list. Jira Filter Any JQL you write, for scopes a space selector cannot express, such as a label across several projects. Either way the scope becomes one JQL string, which is checked against your site before it is saved. That string is everything the project reads. A cost project can therefore cover one or several Jira projects, and a single Jira project can be covered by more than one cost project at once (for example split by cost account). A project reads up to 500 issues. See Limits and behaviour for what happens beyond that and how to split a large project. The Projects table # The home page lists every project you can see. The table fills in progressively: names and statuses appear at once, and the financial columns (Budget, Actual, Remaining, Progress) fill in as each project finishes calculating. Search and filters by status, owner, tags and project attributes. Columns can be shown or hidden with the column configuration at the right edge. Column widths are not remembered after a reload. Sorting: click a column header. Project tabs # Tab What it shows Overview Budget, actual cost, remaining budget, revenue and profit, the monthly cost chart, and schedule, scope and cost progress. Scope Every issue the project counts, with time spent and cost, plus cost by month. Team People, roles and hourly rates. See Rates, roles and the team . Expenses Costs that do not come from logged time. See Expenses . Revenue What the project earns and the profit. See Revenue and profit . Settings General, Rates and revenue, Project Attributes, Sharing and Delete project. Status, tags and timeframe # A project's status is informational and used for filtering: To do, In progress, On hold, Completed or Archived. Tags are free-form words for organising the table. The timeframe (start and end date) is optional and open-ended on either side; if you leave it empty, the Overview shows the dates calculated from the project's issues. Changing the type or currency # You can change a project between monetary and time-based, or change its currency, in Settings. The app asks you to confirm first, because nothing stored is converted : Monetary to time-based: cost and budget are shown in hours. Rates, revenue and billing are kept but hidden. The budget and milestone numbers you entered stay as they are and are now read as hours, so review them. Time-based to monetary: cost is calculated from hourly rates, which are 0 until you set them. The budget and milestone numbers are now read as currency amounts. Changing only the currency changes only the label. The budget, milestones, expenses, fixed revenue and rates keep their numbers and are not converted. Project attributes # Attributes are custom fields (text, number, a pick-one list or a date) that a Jira site administrator defines once under Attributes and attaches to specific projects. An attribute that is attached to no project is hidden everywhere. Once attached, it appears in that project's Settings, can be filled in, and shows as a column in the Projects table. Everyone can see attributes; only site administrators can create, edit or delete them. Deleting a project # Only the owner can delete a project. This removes its rates, team, expenses, revenue entries, budget and milestones; the linked Jira issues are untouched. A portfolio that contained the project keeps working and notes that the member was deleted and is excluded from its totals.

title: Expenses
headings: Add an expense# Recurring expenses# What the tab shows# Editing and deleting#
text: Expenses are costs that worklogs do not capture: software licences, travel, hardware, contractor invoices. They are added to labor cost to give the project's actual cost . On a time-based project, expenses are not part of cost, because cost there is hours. Add an expense # Open the project's Expenses tab and choose to add an expense. Fill in Summary , Amount (greater than 0), Date and, if you like, a free-text Category such as Infrastructure. If cost accounts exist, you can book the expense to an Account (optional). Save. The expense counts toward actual cost immediately. The Add button stays disabled until Summary, Amount and Date are filled in. Dates use Jira's own style, for example Oct 22, 2026 . Recurring expenses # Turn on Recurring for a cost that repeats, such as a monthly hosting fee. Choose how often ( Repeat every N months ) and when it stops: at the project's end date, on a specific date, or after a number of occurrences. A recurring expense projects forward into the forecast the same way actual expenses count backward into cost. If it has to stop at the project's end date and the project has none, the tab says it needs one. What the tab shows # Figure Meaning Actual expenses Recorded so far. Remaining expenses Recurring expenses still to come, until they end. Projected expenses Actual plus remaining. Example: Website redesign A design-tool licence of 200 (one-off) and hosting at 50 per month. After the first month's hosting, actual expenses are 250. Added to the 1,120 labor cost from the quick start , actual cost is 1,370. Editing and deleting # Editors and the owner can edit an expense. Deleting asks for confirmation. Expenses booked to a cost account that is later deleted are shown as "No account". Use Export to XLSX to download the list.

title: Revenue and profit
headings: Two ways to earn revenue# Hourly billing# Fixed price# Fixed revenue entries# Profit and margin#
text: Revenue is available on monetary projects only; a time-based project has no currency to bill in. Turn it on per project under Settings → Rates and revenue → Revenue tracking . Two ways to earn revenue # Hourly billing # Revenue accrues from logged hours at each person's billing rate . The billing rate is chosen with the same order as the cost rate (own, cost account, role, project default), with its own rates and its own default. Fixed price # The project's budget is the contract amount and counts as revenue, whatever hours are logged. Billing rates are hidden. Set the amount as the Budget. Fixed revenue entries # On the Revenue tab you can also add revenue by hand, such as a milestone payment or a licence sold. These fixed revenue entries add to the project's revenue and profit on any monetary project, even with hourly tracking off. A time-based project shows a one-line note instead. Profit and margin # Profit is revenue minus actual cost (labor plus expenses). Margin is profit as a share of revenue. Both are shown next to the cost figures, not in a separate reconciliation step. Example: if Website redesign were a fixed-price project Budget (and so revenue) 6,000. Actual cost is 1,370 (1,120 labor plus 250 expenses). Profit is 4,630 and margin is 77%. Revenue shows 0? Revenue tracking may be off, no billing rate may apply yet (a banner says so), or a fixed-price project has no budget. See Troubleshooting .

title: Budget and milestones
headings: Budget# Milestones: a plan of spend over time# Reading the Overview#
text: Budget # A budget is optional. Set it in Settings → General → Schedule and budget . On a monetary project the budget is an amount in the project's currency; on a time-based project it is a number of hours. With no budget, remaining budget and progress show a dash instead of a misleading figure. On a fixed-price project the budget is also the project's revenue. See Revenue and profit . Milestones: a plan of spend over time # Under the budget, Set budget milestones lets you plan how much should have been spent by given dates. Each milestone is a date and a cumulative amount, so every amount is the running total: amounts may not fall as dates advance, no amount may exceed the budget, two milestones cannot share a date, and there can be at most 24. On a time-based project the milestones are hours. Example: Website redesign Budget 6,000. Milestones: 1 Jun 1,000, 1 Jul 3,000, 1 Aug 5,000. If actual cost on 1 Jul is 3,400, the Overview reads "Plan to date: 3,000, spent 3,400 — 400 ahead of plan", in red. Reading the Overview # The Overview shows schedule , scope and cost progress side by side, so an overrun appears against the same timeline that causes it, not just as one red number. Progress bar Measures Schedule How far through the project's timeframe today is. Scope Issues in a done status category out of all issues scanned, with the number remaining. Cost (or Hours) Actual cost against the budget, with the amount remaining or the amount over budget. Two lines can appear under the bars: Plan to date (when milestones exist): what the plan says should have been spent by now, what was spent, and the difference, shown as "ahead of plan" (spent more than planned), "under plan" or "exactly on plan". Forecast by the end date (when recurring expenses exist): actual cost plus the recurring expenses still to come, and by how much that would exceed the budget. The monthly cost chart shows labor and expenses per month, and an Accounts card splits cost by account category such as CAPEX and OPEX. If the scope was capped at the 500-issue limit, the Overview says so under the figures.

title: Cost accounts
headings: What an account holds# How an account is applied to a project# Who can manage accounts#
text: A cost account groups work for cost purposes: capitalised versus operating spend, a client, a cost centre. Unlike a Jira custom field, an account is defined by a JQL filter, so no field has to be added to your issues. What an account holds # Field Notes Name and Key Both must be unique across the site. Category Billable, Capitalized (CAPEX), Operating (OPEX) or Other. JQL Which issues belong to the account. It is checked when you save it. Cost rate, Billing rate Optional hourly rates for work on the account's issues. They can start on a date; see Rates that change over time . Lead, Customer, Contact Optional descriptive fields. Status Open or Closed. Informational: it filters the list but does not switch the account off. How an account is applied to a project # For each project, the account's JQL is combined (AND) with the project's own scope, and the matching issues are found in the same scan that computes the report. An account's rate applies to work on its issues. It beats a role's rate and the project default, but not a person's own rate. An issue that matches more than one account goes to the account created first, so every worklog has exactly one rate. If an account's JQL later stops being valid (a deleted field, for example), the account is skipped rather than breaking the report. Account rates are plain numbers applied as-is in each project's own currency. There is no conversion. Expenses can be booked to an account, which is how the Overview's Accounts card and the "by account" report split cost. Who can manage accounts # Accounts are site-wide setup, like attributes and the role library. Only Jira site administrators can create, edit or delete them; everyone can see them. Accounts are managed under Setup → Accounts , with a switch between Accounts and Customers views. You can create up to 20 accounts, because each one costs an extra Jira search every time a project is calculated.

title: Portfolios
headings: Create and fill a portfolio# The two tabs# Mixed currencies and time-based projects# Deleted and capped members# Access#
text: A portfolio groups cost projects so you can see their combined cost, budget and schedule. Open Portfolios in the sidebar to list them, and click a portfolio's name to open it. Create and fill a portfolio # Choose Create portfolio , name it and, optionally, describe it. Open it, go to the Summary tab and use Add projects . A searchable table with checkboxes lets you add or remove several at once. Only projects you can see can be added. The two tabs # Tab What it shows Summary Combined figures (total cost, total budget, team size, project count), the member projects with their own status, dates and revenue, and Export to XLSX . Configuration Name, description, owner and projects, plus the portfolio's sharing. The Summary shows its totals once every member has been calculated. Each member's figures arrive separately, so a slow project never blocks the page. Mixed currencies and time-based projects # Hours always add up. Money adds up only across monetary projects that share one currency. With mixed currencies, or only time-based members, the money totals are left out and the page says so, rather than adding unlike units. Amounts are not converted between currencies. Deleted and capped members # If a member project is deleted, the portfolio still loads and notes that the member was excluded from the totals. If a member hit the 500-issue limit, a warning names that project, so you know which total is incomplete. Access # A portfolio is private to its owner by default . The owner can share it with named people as read-only viewers . There is no "everyone" option and no editor level. Only the owner can delete the portfolio, add or remove projects and edit its description. See Sharing and ownership .

title: Reports
headings: Create a report# The Reports list# Filters in the result view# Export# Portfolio reports#
text: A report covers one project or portfolio over a timeframe . Unlike the Overview, which shows everything logged, a report lets you choose the period and how to slice it. Create a report # Open Reports in the sidebar and choose New report . Give it a Name , then pick the Project or portfolio and the Timeframe . Choose a Report type . For By period also choose the Breakdown : by week or by month. Choose Create . The report is saved and opens. Report type Rows are By period Weeks or months in the timeframe. By person One row per person, with a total. By account One row per cost account (including "No account"), so you can see CAPEX versus OPEX for the period. Totals are shown as tiles: hours, labor cost, expenses and total cost. A time-based project reports hours only. The Reports list # Saved reports appear as cards with their name, type, project or portfolio and period, and a search box above. Click a report's name to open it (a read-only view of the result). Use Edit to change its settings and Update to save, or Delete (with confirmation). Filters in the result view # When a report is open you can narrow it by Person and by Account . These filters are for looking, not part of the saved report. Expenses cannot be attributed to a person, so a person filter shows labor only; an account filter keeps expenses booked to that account. Export # Use Export to XLSX to download the current result as a spreadsheet. Portfolio reports # A portfolio report is each member project's report for the period, merged. Hours add up. Money adds up only across monetary members that share one currency; with mixed currencies, or only time-based members, the cost columns are left out and the page says so. Members that cannot be loaded (for example, a deleted project) are listed and left out. If a member hit the 500-issue limit, the warning names it. A report always reads Jira live and is not cached like the Overview, so a large project's report can take a moment to open.

title: Sharing and ownership
headings: Projects# Adding a person# Transferring ownership# Portfolios# Site-wide setup# Locked out?#
text: Projects # Every cost project has an owner (its creator at first), a general access setting and an optional list of people. Open Settings → Sharing (owners only) to change it. General access Meaning Everyone Anyone using the app can open the project, view-only. This is the default for a new project. Restricted Only the owner and the people you name can open it. You can add people as Viewer or Editor , up to 50. Naming someone lifts them above the general setting: an Editor can change a restricted or an "everyone" project alike. Adding a person # Under Add a person , type at least two letters of a name or email. The search is live and lists existing users of your Jira site . It does not send invitations or email, so someone new must first be invited to the Jira site (Jira settings → User management → Invite user). App accounts are not offered, only people. Transferring ownership # The owner can hand the project to someone else under Transfer ownership . The new owner takes full control; the previous owner stays on as an editor rather than being locked out. Portfolios # Portfolios are simpler. A portfolio is private to its owner by default, or shared with named people as read-only viewers (Configuration → Sharing). There is no "everyone" option and no editor level. Only the owner can delete the portfolio, add or remove its projects, and edit its description. Site-wide setup # Cost accounts, attributes and the role library are not tied to one project. Everyone can see them; only Jira site administrators can create, edit or delete them. Locked out? # If a restricted project's owner has left, a Jira site administrator can still open it. The app shows a notice that they are seeing it as a site admin, and they can repair its Sharing so it never ends up with nobody able to manage it.

title: Limits and behaviour
headings: Limits# If a project is over 500 issues# Behaviour#
text: Limits # What Limit What happens at the limit Issues read per cost project 500 The page says "first 500 of about N issues" and the totals are incomplete. Split the project (below). Cost accounts on the site 20 Creating a 21st is refused. Each account costs an extra Jira search per project calculation. Role name length 60 Refused. Names must also be unique within a project, ignoring case. Milestones per project 24 Refused. People named in a project's sharing 50 Refused. Calculated figures are kept ~15 min Recomputed after that, or immediately after a change that affects them. If a project is over 500 issues # The 500-issue limit is deliberate, sized for small and medium teams. A bigger scope still works, but only the first 500 issues count and the page says so (Overview, Scope and Reports all show the warning, with the real size when Jira can tell). To get complete figures: Split by Jira space. If the scope covers several spaces, make one cost project per space and group them in a portfolio . Narrow by period. Add a date condition to the JQL, for example AND created >= "2026-01-01" , and keep a separate project for older work. Behaviour # Topic How it behaves Currency A property of each project. Amounts are never converted. A portfolio or report adds money only across projects with the same currency. Rates Non-negative numbers. Empty means "use the next level", 0 is a real rate. A rate can start on a date; with no date it applies to all hours. Worklog date The day the worklog was logged for, as Jira stores it. Rates are matched to this date. Type or currency change Nothing is converted; the app asks you to confirm first. Date format Shown in Jira's own style, for example Oct 22, 2026 . Typed dates also accept YYYY-MM-DD . Reports Read Jira live (not cached) for the chosen timeframe. Exports XLSX files, generated from what is on screen. CSV export was removed. Jira data Only read, never changed. See Privacy .

title: Permissions and access
headings: Who can do what# Permissions the app asks for#
text: Who can do what # Access is decided per project. See Sharing and ownership for how people are given a level. Action Viewer Editor Owner Site admin Open a project and read its figures Yes Yes Yes Yes, even if not shared with them Change settings, rates, team, expenses, revenue, budget, milestones No Yes Yes Yes, as owner Change sharing, transfer ownership, delete the project No No Yes Yes, as owner Create a project Anyone using the app; the creator becomes its owner. Portfolios Action Viewer Owner Open it and read its figures Yes Yes Add or remove projects, edit the description, share it, delete it No Yes Site-wide setup Resource See it Create, edit, delete Cost accounts Everyone Jira site administrators Attributes Everyone Jira site administrators Role library Everyone Jira site administrators Reports A report's data is limited by the project it reads: you only see figures for projects you can open. Hourly rates are tied to named people and can reveal compensation-related information. Who sees a project's rates is controlled by that project's sharing settings, and nothing in the app shows one project's rates to someone without access to it. Permissions the app asks for # The app requests four Forge permissions and nothing else: Permission Used for read:jira-work Searching issues and reading their worklogs and dates, listing Jira projects, and checking whether you are a site administrator. read:jira-user Showing people's names and finding users to add as members or to share with. storage:app Keeping the app's own data (projects, rates, expenses) in Forge storage. report:personal-data Atlassian's weekly personal data check: the app tells Atlassian which account IDs it holds, and Atlassian answers which accounts were closed or changed. See Privacy policy . Jira is only ever read, never written to. Requests to Jira run as the person using the app. Cost Tracker declares no external network access and no web triggers. Details: Privacy policy and Security policy .

title: Glossary
text: Actual cost Labor cost plus expenses recorded so far. On a time-based project, actual hours. Billing rate What a client is charged per hour for a person's work. Separate from the cost rate, and used only when hourly revenue is on. Budget An optional target for a project: an amount in its currency, or hours on a time-based project. On a fixed-price project it is also the revenue. Cost account A named bucket of work (for example CAPEX, OPEX or a client) defined by JQL. It can carry its own rates and receive expenses. Managed site-wide by Jira administrators. Cost project The app's own entity: a scope plus everything that hangs off it (rates, team, expenses, revenue, budget). Not a copy of a Jira project. Cost rate What a person costs the business per hour. Default hourly rate The project's fallback rate, used when no own, account or role rate applies. A new project starts at 0. Effective from The date a rate starts to apply. Hours logged on or after it use the new rate; earlier hours keep their old one. Expense A cost that is not logged time: a licence, travel, a contractor invoice. One-off or recurring. Fixed price A revenue mode where the project's budget is its revenue regardless of hours logged. JQL Jira Query Language. Used to define a cost project's scope and a cost account's issues. Labor cost The sum of every worklog's hours times its rate. Margin Profit as a share of revenue. Milestone A date and a cumulative planned spend. Together they form the plan the Overview compares actual cost with. Monetary-based A project type whose cost and budget are in a currency, computed from hourly rates. Period (of a rate) A stretch of time during which a rate has one value. A rate with several periods has a history. Portfolio A group of cost projects with a combined view of cost, budget and team. Profit Revenue minus actual cost. Role A named group of people in one project with a shared cost and billing rate. Scope What a cost project reads: one or more Jira spaces, or a JQL filter. It resolves to one JQL string. Space (Jira space) Jira's name for a project container. "Jira space" and "Jira project" mean the same thing in these docs, to tell them apart from a cost project. Time-based A project type whose cost and budget are in hours. It uses no rates and has no revenue. Worklog A record of time logged on a Jira issue. Cost Tracker reads these; nobody logs time in the app.

title: Troubleshooting
headings: Numbers# Cost shows 0# Totals look incomplete or "first 500 of about N issues"# I changed a rate and old numbers moved# Overview and a report show different numbers# A figure did not update after I logged time in Jira# Revenue shows 0# Portfolio totals are blank or missing# Access# I cannot open or edit a project# I cannot find a person to add# I cannot create or edit accounts, attributes or library roles# A project I expected is not in my portfolio or list# Setup# Where is the app?# The scope is rejected when I save# A cost account stopped applying# Still stuck?#
text: Find the symptom, check the cause, follow the fix. If nothing here helps, see support . Numbers # Cost shows 0 # Check What to do Is there an "Hourly rates are not set" banner? A new monetary project's default hourly rate is 0. Set a Default hourly rate in Settings → Rates and revenue, or rates per person or role on the Team tab. Do the project's issues have logged time? Cost comes only from worklogs on issues in the scope. Check the scope in Settings and that the issues really have time logged. Is the project time-based? Then there is no money, only hours. Switch to monetary in Settings if you need cost (see changing the type ). Is a rate set to 0 on purpose? 0 is a real rate (unpaid work) and does not trigger the banner. Clear the field to fall back to the next level. Totals look incomplete or "first 500 of about N issues" # Cause: a project reads at most 500 issues. Fix: split the project by Jira space or by period. See Limits and behaviour . I changed a rate and old numbers moved # Cause: the change had no Effective from date, so it applied to all hours. Fix: to keep history, set the rate again with an Effective from date (a rate can have several periods); set the earlier rate on its own start date. See Rates that change over time . Overview and a report show different numbers # The Overview totals everything logged; a report covers the timeframe you chose. A report filtered by person shows labor only, because expenses cannot be attributed to a person. The Overview is kept for about 15 minutes; a report reads Jira live. A worklog logged in the last minutes may appear in the report first. A figure did not update after I logged time in Jira # Calculated figures are kept for about 15 minutes. Wait, or change something in the project (any rate, role or setting) to make it recompute straight away. Revenue shows 0 # Revenue tracking may be off (Settings → Rates and revenue). With hourly billing, a banner says when no billing rate applies yet. Set a Default billing rate or billing rates. With fixed price, revenue is the project's budget ; set one. Time-based projects have no revenue. Portfolio totals are blank or missing # Money adds up only across monetary projects with the same currency . With mixed currencies, or only time-based members, the money totals are left out and the page says so. Hours still add up. Access # I cannot open or edit a project # Access is per project: owner, editor, viewer or none. Ask the project's owner to change its sharing (Settings → Sharing), or a Jira site administrator if the owner has left. A viewer can read but not change anything. I cannot find a person to add # The search lists existing users of your Jira site only, and needs at least two letters. The app cannot invite people or send email: invite them to the Jira site first (Jira settings → User management → Invite user), then search again. App accounts are not offered. I cannot create or edit accounts, attributes or library roles # These are site-wide and limited to Jira site administrators . Everyone can see them. Ask an administrator. A project I expected is not in my portfolio or list # It may be restricted and not shared with you. If it was deleted, a portfolio notes that the member was excluded. Only projects you can see can be added to a portfolio. Setup # Where is the app? # Open Cost Tracker from the Apps menu in the Jira sidebar. It is one global page; it does not appear inside individual Jira projects. The scope is rejected when I save # The JQL is validated against your site. Fix the query (a misspelt field, an unknown project key) and save again. A project you cannot see in Jira is not found either. A cost account stopped applying # If an account's JQL stops being valid (a field was deleted, for example), the account is skipped instead of breaking reports. Edit the account's JQL to fix it. Still stuck? # Write to info@vudia.site with the project name, what you expected, what you saw, and (if you can) a screenshot.

title: FAQ and support
text: Does it replace Jira's own time tracking? No. It reads the worklogs your team already logs in Jira. There is no second place to log time. Does the app change anything in Jira? No. It only reads issues, worklogs and users. It never creates, edits or comments on an issue. Can one Jira project belong to more than one cost project? Yes. Scope is defined independently each time, so the same Jira project can be covered by several cost projects at once, for example one per cost account. Time-based or monetary: can I change it later? Yes, in Settings, and the app asks you to confirm first. Nothing is converted: the budget and milestone numbers keep their values and are simply read as hours or as currency amounts, so review them. See changing the type or currency . A person's rate went up. How do I keep last month's cost? Set the new rate with an Effective from date. Hours before that date keep the old rate. See Rates that change over time . Why does the app say hourly rates are not set? Logged time is being counted at 0 only because no rate applies to it. A new monetary project starts with a default rate of 0. A rate you set to 0 on purpose does not trigger the banner. Why does a person show a rate I never entered? It comes from a lower level: a cost account, their role, or the project default. The label next to the rate says which; "mixed" means an account's rate covered only some of their worklogs. Is there a limit on project size? Yes: 500 issues per project. This is a deliberate limit. See Limits and behaviour for how to split a large project. Are different currencies converted? No. Each project has one currency, and a portfolio or report adds money only across projects that share it. Can I export data? Yes, to XLSX, from expenses, fixed revenue, portfolios and reports. Where does the data live? In Forge storage on your own Atlassian site. See the privacy policy for exactly what is kept. Support # Questions, bug reports or feature requests: info@vudia.site . To help us answer quickly, include the project name, what you expected, what you saw and a screenshot if possible. Security reports go to the address on the security page .

title: What's new
headings: October 2026# 11 October# 9 October# 8 October# 1 October# Late September 2026#
text: October 2026 # 11 October # Rates can change over time. Every rate (a person's, a role's, a cost account's and the project default) can now start on a date. Hours logged before the date keep their old rate, so a raise no longer reprices past months. Each period records who set it and when, and a history window lists them. Leaving the date empty works as before: the rate applies to all hours. See Rates that change over time . "Hourly rates are not set" banner. Overview, Team and Revenue now say when logged time is counted at 0 only because no rate applies yet. Confirmation before changing a project's type or currency. The window explains that nothing stored is converted. Clearer limit warning. When a project has more than 500 issues, the page now shows "first 500 of about N issues" and how to split the project. The portfolio Timeline tab was removed; a portfolio now has Summary and Configuration tabs. Portfolio pages show their cards and member projects straight away and fill in figures as each project finishes calculating. People pickers no longer list app accounts. Attributes attach to specific projects and appear only on those. 9 October # Cost Tracker is now only on the global Apps page. It no longer appears inside individual Jira projects. The Projects table appears at once and fills in its financial columns row by row, so a slow project never blocks the page. 8 October # Reports reworked into a list of saved reports, a read-only result view and an edit form. Editing a saved report now updates it instead of risking a duplicate. People search auto-triggers after two letters, with no Search button. This documentation site, privacy policy and security policy were published. 1 October # Recurring expenses can repeat every N months and stop at the project's end date, a specific date or after a number of occurrences. Dates use Jira's own style, for example Oct 22, 2026 . Export to XLSX replaced the old copy-and-paste CSV export, on expenses, fixed revenue, portfolios and reports. Late September 2026 # Portfolio access: portfolios are private to their owner and can be shared with named people as read-only viewers. Transfer ownership: a project owner can hand a project to someone else and stays on as an editor. Site-wide setup (accounts, attributes, role library) can be changed only by Jira site administrators. Revenue tab, fixed revenue entries and a portfolio Configuration tab.

title: Privacy policy
headings: Summary# What it reads from Jira# What it writes to Jira# What it stores# Rates are sensitive data# Personal data and closed accounts# Retention & deletion# Where data is stored# Logs# Analytics & tracking# Your rights# Changes to this policy# Contact#
text: Summary # Cost Tracker is built on Atlassian Forge and runs entirely on Atlassian's infrastructure — it has no servers of its own and makes no outbound network call to anything outside Atlassian. We do not operate any system that receives your data, and we cannot see the data your site holds in the app. The app reads issues, worklogs, and user names using the permissions of whoever is using it, and stores the projects, rates, expenses and reports your users enter in Forge storage, scoped to your own site. What it reads from Jira # Depending on what a feature needs, and always live, using the viewer's own Jira permissions: Issue key, summary, status, type, created/due dates, and the status-category change date, for issues matching a cost project's own scope Worklogs on those issues — author account ID and display name, time spent, and date The list of Jira projects on your site, to populate the project/space picker User search results, to add people to a team, share a project, or transfer ownership The caller's own account profile, and whether they hold the site's ADMINISTER permission, to gate site-wide setup screens None of it is copied anywhere outside your site. What it writes to Jira # Nothing. The app never creates, edits, transitions, or comments on a Jira issue — it only reads. What it stores # In Forge storage, scoped to your site: the cost projects, portfolios, roles, hourly rates, team memberships, expenses, revenue entries, budgets, milestones, cost accounts, custom attributes and saved reports that your users create, plus a short-lived cache of computed report totals (recomputed every ~15 minutes, or sooner after a change that affects the numbers). passwords API tokens payment details issue content beyond what's listed above Rates are sensitive data # Hourly cost and billing rates are tied to named people and can reveal compensation-related information. Who can see a project's rates is controlled by that project's own sharing settings — set, and changeable only, by its owner. There's no feature that surfaces one project's rates to someone who isn't given access to that project. Personal data and closed accounts # The only personal data the app stores is the Atlassian account ID and display name of people your users name in it: a project's owner and the people it is shared with, team members and their roles, the person a rate belongs to and who last changed it, a cost account's lead, a portfolio's owner and viewers, and the person chosen in a saved "by person" report. It stores no email address, password, payment detail or token. As Atlassian requires of every app that stores personal data, the app checks this once a week through Atlassian's Personal data reporting API: it sends the account IDs it holds and Atlassian answers which accounts were closed or had their profile changed. Nothing else is sent, and no data leaves Atlassian's infrastructure. Closed account: the person is erased. Their team memberships, their own rates, their place in sharing lists and their name as an owner, lead or editor are removed, and a saved report filtered on them loses that filter. Rates, costs and projects themselves are kept; a project or portfolio that had them as owner is left without an owner, which a Jira site administrator can then manage. Changed profile: the stored display name is dropped, and filled in again the next time someone opens a screen that shows it, by looking it up as that user. The weekly check itself never reads Jira. Computed report totals, which contain people's names, are discarded whenever either happens and are rebuilt on the next view. The app writes only counts to its logs, never an account ID or a name. Retention & deletion # Data stays in your site's Forge storage until your users delete it in the app, or until the app is uninstalled. Deleting a cost project removes its own rates, team, expenses, revenue, budget and milestones; it does not retroactively scrub it from a portfolio's history, which instead shows a "member was deleted" note. Removal of storage after uninstall follows Atlassian's own Forge retention policy. Where data is stored # Inside Atlassian's own Forge storage platform, in the same data residency as the rest of your Jira site. Nothing leaves Atlassian's infrastructure — the app declares no permission to call any external service. Logs # The app writes a diagnostic log line only when something fails unexpectedly. These logs are not used to reconstruct rates, expenses, or other figures you've entered. Analytics & tracking # None. The app contains no analytics, no tracking pixels, no advertising, and no third-party scripts of any kind. Your rights # Because we hold no copy of your data outside your own Forge storage, requests to access, correct, or delete it are handled directly inside the app and Jira by your site administrators — sharing settings determine who can reach a given project's data, and a site admin can always reach it. If you have a question we haven't answered here, contact us using the details below. Changes to this policy # If what the app reads, writes, or stores changes, this page changes with it. Contact # info@vudia.site

title: Security policy
headings: Architecture and hosting# Data we handle# Authentication and access control# Internal security practices# Vulnerability management# Incident response# Business continuity# Third-party risk# Compliance# Policy review#
text: Architecture and hosting # Cost Tracker is built entirely on Atlassian Forge, in UI Kit (not Custom UI) — its interface is rendered by the platform itself, not by code we serve. It has no servers, databases, or infrastructure of its own: it stores no data outside Atlassian, and its manifest declares no permission to make an outbound network call to anything other than Atlassian's own APIs. TLS, HSTS, DDoS protection, encryption at rest, physical security, and patching of the underlying platform are Atlassian's responsibility, not ours — and are covered by Atlassian's own SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certifications. Data we handle # The app reads issue and worklog data, live, using the viewer's own Jira permissions, scoped to whichever cost project they're looking at — and shows it straight back to them, aggregated into cost, budget and revenue figures. None of it is copied anywhere else. What's written to Forge's key-value storage is the configuration your users enter directly — project names and scopes, hourly rates, expenses, budgets, report settings — plus a short-lived cache of computed totals. Full detail, including exactly what is and isn't kept, is in the privacy policy . The app holds no permission to create, edit, transition, or comment on an issue — it cannot write to Jira at all. Authentication and access control # There is no independent login system. Every request runs as the signed-in Jira user, authenticated by Forge through their existing Jira session — we never collect, transmit, or store Atlassian usernames, passwords, or API tokens. Within the app, every project-scoped action is additionally checked against that project's own sharing setting (owner, editor, viewer, or restricted) before it runs, server-side, using the caller's account ID as supplied by Forge rather than anything the client claims. Access is bounded by the scopes declared in the app's manifest: read:jira-work search issues, read worklogs and dates, list Jira projects, check site-admin status read:jira-user show people's names, search users to add as team members or share a project with storage:app the app's own Forge key-value store report:personal-data Atlassian's Personal data reporting API: a weekly check of which stored account IDs belong to closed or changed accounts No Jira write scope is declared anywhere in the manifest. The app never acts as itself on a user's behalf: every Jira call is made as the signed-in user ( asUser ), and the weekly personal data check makes no Jira call at all. Internal security practices # Cost Tracker is developed by a small team at Vudia. Multi-factor authentication is enforced on the Atlassian Developer Console account and on the GitHub account ( Dbelokon-cpu ) that hosts both this documentation site and the app's source. Source code is kept in a private GitHub repository — not publicly browsable — with the same MFA-protected account controlling access. Dependabot is enabled on that repository: alerts and automated security fixes for known vulnerabilities, plus a weekly check for routine dependency updates. Credentials are kept in a password manager; passwords are not shared or reused across services. Every change runs through an automated test suite and a linter in CI before it ships. Vulnerability management # Development follows OWASP Top 10 guidance — every project-scoped resolver is required to pass through the app's own access check, enforced by a test that fails the build if a new one is added without it. Dependabot watches the dependency tree continuously and opens a pull request when a known vulnerability is published. We are evaluating enrolment in the Atlassian Marketplace-managed security bug bounty program (via Bugcrowd). In the meantime, reports are handled directly — see contacts below — and we follow the Marketplace's own SLA: 10 days for Critical severity, 28 days for High severity. Incident response # Investigate the report and confirm scope — what's affected, and how. Notify Atlassian within 24 hours via a priority (P1) support ticket if the platform itself is implicated. Contain the issue and ship a remediation. Notify affected customers directly if any of their data was involved. Run a post-incident review and record what changes as a result. Purpose Contact Response Security report security@vudia.site Prioritised General support info@vudia.site Two business days Privacy questions See the privacy policy Business continuity # Because the app has no infrastructure of its own, its availability depends entirely on Atlassian Forge's own SLA and uptime — there is no independent server, database, or backup process for it to fail separately from Atlassian's platform. Third-party risk # Atlassian is the only third party involved: it provides storage, hosting, and operations, and is certified under SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001. The app uses no analytics, no subprocessors, and no external APIs — its manifest declares no permission to reach anything outside Atlassian. Compliance # We do not hold independent security certifications (SOC 2, ISO 27001, or similar) at this time. The app inherits the controls of Atlassian's own certified platform, and is built to comply with the Atlassian Marketplace's security requirements for Cloud apps. Policy review # This policy is reviewed at least once a year, and sooner if the app's architecture, data handling, or team changes materially.
